name: sse4_crc32
workload: Node.js native-addon benchmark: CRC-32C over a fixed-size buffer and over multiple random-length buffers, 10000 iterations each
claimed_speedup: Native SSE4.2 CRC-32C ~2.5x faster than native table-based CRC-32C (4.319ms vs 10.726ms per 10000 iterations, fixed buffer); ~3.7x faster on random-length buffers (60.194ms vs 225.460ms)
hardware: MacBook Air, Intel Core i7 (exact model unspecified), 16GB RAM
stars_or_usage: 133 stars; distributed as the npm package sse4_crc32
tradeoffs: Requires SSE4.2 hardware (falls back to software otherwise); computes CRC-32C (Castagnoli polynomial), not the standard CRC-32 (zlib) polynomial; ships as a Node.js native addon requiring node-gyp compilation
caveats: Benchmark numbers date to 2013, no compiler/build flags stated, CPU model unspecified beyond 'Intel Core i7'; the comparison is against the project's own software fallback rather than directly against zlib's crc32(); discovered via a 2019 fork (Voxer/sse4_crc32, 2 stars) of this canonical repo, which itself has had no commits since 2023 (abandoned)
found_via: Hacker News: query 'crc32c hardware' surfaced https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=6817084 (Hardware-accelerated CRC-32 library) and https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=6837489 (engineering.voxer.com blog post), both linking to github.com/Voxer/sse4_crc32, a fork of anandsuresh/sse4_crc32

name: fasthex
workload: Hex-dumping large files (1.5 GiB and 69 GiB) to /dev/null, wall-clock time measured with hyperfine (3 warmup runs)
claimed_speedup: 0.78s vs xxd 43.62s (55.5x slower), hexyl --color=never 53.14s (67.6x slower), hexyl 104.93s (133.5x slower), hexdump 116.03s (147.5x slower) on a 1.5 GiB file; ~1 minute vs hexyl's ~1h30m on a 69 GiB file
hardware: Intel i5-7700T, 16GB DDR4 RAM, Samsung 990 Pro NVMe SSD
tradeoffs: Relies on Linux-specific I/O tricks (mmap, vmsplice/splice, MADV_SEQUENTIAL) plus rayon parallelism and AVX2/SSE4.1/SSSE3 SIMD formatting; falls back to write_all when splice is unavailable (e.g. a tty); portability to macOS/Windows for the zero-copy path is unclear
caveats: No compiler/build flags stated (Rust, release mode assumed); benchmark driver script not published, only a testing-conditions gist with hardware info; multipliers >50x are large and driven partly by comparison tools' unoptimized I/O rather than pure hex-encoding throughput, so tier is capped at C per the >50x rule
found_via: Hacker News: query 'Show HN fast hex' surfaced https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48719795 (Show HN: A fast hex dumper, written in Rust)
